clue.text: World poem rewrite for 16 creation

indicators.note: to rewrite the words is to recast them, so their letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the printed fodder words, which need one more I to give the setter's intended letters

explanation.surface: A plan to recast a poem about the world as a novelist's character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrite' signals an anagram, but WORLD POEM gives only nine letters; the name needs one more I, so the clue as printed is a letter short. 16 is POWELL, whose Dance to the Music of Time features Kenneth Widmerpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Widmerpool is the scheming figure invented by Anthony Powell in his novel sequence, so he is that writer's creation.

clue.text: Reckless character of England's Fielding

explanation.surface: A rash figure in the novels of England's Henry Fielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Reckless means untamed or rash; Jonathan is the criminal title figure of Fielding's satire Jonathan Wild.

clue.text: Pastoral poet uses cart with heavy load

parts.note: a dray is a low cart for heavy goods such as beer barrels
a ton is a large weight, a heavy load

explanation.surface: A poet of country life is pictured hauling a laden wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Drayton (1563-1631) wrote the pastoral collection The Shepherd's Garland.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Drayton wrote eclogues and pastorals in the Elizabethan style, a poet of shepherds and the countryside.

clue.text: Spenserian song adapted by Gustafson in wartime

explanation.surface: A Renaissance wedding ode reworked by a modern poet during the war.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's wedding ode bears this title; the Canadian poet Ralph Gustafson adapted it as Epithalamium in Time of War.

clue.text: Composer indicates heathen in one

parts.note: a pagan is a heathen, someone outside the main faiths
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone claims a musician is an unbeliever among one group.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolo Paganini was the Italian violinist who wrote the famous Caprices, a composer as well as performer.

clue.text: Preferred to lemon with fish by Carol Shields

definitions.text: Preferred to lemon with fish by Carol Shields

parts.words: Preferred to lemon with fish by Carol Shields
parts.note: seems to be about a garnish for seafood, but refers to the colour in the title of Carol Shields's story collection about a fish

explanation.surface: A novelist's choice of citrus to serve with seafood.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol Shields, the Canadian-American novelist, published the collection Various Miracles and also The Orange Fish (1989); the clue names the fruit chosen over lemon.
explanation.definitionFit: Shields titled her 1989 story collection after a fish of this colour, so the fruit is the one she chose rather than lemon.

clue.text: Goddess from the other Athenian pantheon

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of a run of the clue's words

explanation.surface: A deity drawn from the rival Greek city's collection of gods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to a run of letters inside 'other Athenian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeus's wife was queen of the Olympian deities, the goddess of marriage.

clue.text: University on continent briefly reveals Gorgon

indicators.note: on here means the university is set after the shortened continent, building the name in that order
briefly means the word is cut short, losing its last letters

parts.note: Europe is a continent
Yale is a famous American university

explanation.surface: An American college abroad unveils a snake-haired monster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' trims the continent to its first three letters; 'on' places the college after them. 'reveals' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Euryale was one of the three Gorgon sisters, with Stheno and the mortal Medusa.

clue.text: Uncontrolled carnal glee shown by hypocrite with murderous wife

indicators.note: uncontrolled means running wild, so the letters of the following words are scrambled

explanation.surface: A two-faced man's lust is exposed, and his wife turns killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncontrolled' signals an anagram of CARNAL GLEE. In Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles Angel rejects Tess for her past despite his own, and she later kills Alec.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Angel Clare condemns Tess for a past like his own, a hypocrite, and she goes on to stab Alec d'Urberville.

clue.text: Top of the bill in Magdalen, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters may be arranged otherwise, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: The star performer at an Oxford college production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of IN MAGDALEN; Magdalen is an Oxford college, suggesting a student play.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal male actor gets top billing on a theatre poster.

clue.text: Clasped by Tennyson's eagle

parts.note: recalls the opening line of Tennyson's short poem The Eagle, where the bird grips a rocky height with crooked hands

explanation.surface: What the bird holds in a Victorian poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's eagle grips a steep rock face high above the sea, the opening image of the poem.

clue.text: An especially venomous Sayers offering

parts.note: describes a deadly dose while naming the title of Dorothy L. Sayers's 1930 Lord Peter Wimsey novel

explanation.surface: A crime writer serves up something lethal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sayers's 1930 mystery, in which Harriet Vane is tried for murder by arsenic, has this title, which also means a potent toxin.

clue.text: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)

definitions.text: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)

parts.words: "Most people have a furious — to talk about themselves" (Somerset Maugham)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap; the missing word is a strong craving or urge

explanation.surface: Maugham's remark on how eager people are to speak of themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a word for a restless desire, a craving that must be satisfied.

clue.text: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach

definitions.text: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach

parts.words: Auden said that birds turn their head at her approach
parts.note: recalls Auden's verse for the 1936 GPO documentary about the overnight postal train from London to Scotland

explanation.surface: A poet's observation of birds watching a woman arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'her' is a train: in Auden's poem 'Birds turn their heads as she approaches'.
explanation.definitionFit: Auden's poem for the GPO film follows the overnight postal train; birds turn their heads as it passes.

clue.text: Izaak does not start at gated section of river, we are told, in Kingsley's work

indicators.note: printed 'star' is an OCR slip for 'start': the name loses its opening letter

parts.note: Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler

indicators.note: we are told means the next piece is a word heard spoken, not written

parts.note: a lock is a section of river closed off by gates to raise or lower boats

explanation.surface: The famous angler hesitates by a river lock in a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star' is an OCR slip for 'start': 'does not start' drops the angler's initial; 'we are told' gives the river feature's sound with a silent final E. Kingsley's 1850 novel follows a Chartist tailor-poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Alton Locke, Tailor and Poet is Charles Kingsley's 1850 novel, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Early poet from German director's territory

parts.note: Fritz Lang was the German film director of Metropolis
land is territory, ground held

explanation.surface: A medieval poet emerges from a film-maker's domain.
explanation.walkthrough: William Langland wrote Piers Plowman in the 14th century.
explanation.definitionFit: William Langland, author of Piers Plowman, was a 14th-century poet, early in English literature.

clue.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

definitions.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

parts.words: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing
parts.note: seems to describe a parent's worries, but refers to the first novel of a twelve-volume sequence

explanation.surface: A man worried from the start about how children are raised.
explanation.walkthrough: A Question of Upbringing (1951) opens Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time, so it occupied him early in the sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell began his novel sequence with A Question of Upbringing, so that book occupied him first.

clue.text: Prohibition at French town for prominent Irish writer

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition
ville is the French word for town

explanation.surface: A ban on a French town is linked to a celebrated Irish author.
explanation.walkthrough: John Banville is the Booker-winning Irish novelist of The Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: John Banville, author of The Sea, is a leading contemporary novelist from Ireland.

clue.text: Giant and some overactors present old characters

parts.note: Og, king of Bashan, was a giant in the Old Testament
hams are actors who overact

explanation.surface: A giant and a troupe of hammy actors put on an old play.
explanation.walkthrough: Ogham is the ancient Irish alphabet of strokes cut on stone edges.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham letters are the ancient Celtic script carved on standing stones, so they are old written symbols.

clue.text: Novel sort of rogue

parts.note: seems to mean a new kind of scoundrel, but points to the surname in the title of Hugh Walpole's novel Rogue ...

explanation.surface: A new type of villain.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Walpole's 1930 novel Rogue Herries opens his Lake District family saga; 'Novel' is the book, not new.
explanation.definitionFit: Walpole's book Rogue Herries names its scoundrel hero by this family name, so it is the rogue of a novel.

clue.text: Josephine Tay's was Time's

parts.note: points to Josephine Tey's 1951 detective novel in which a hospitalised inspector investigates Richard III

explanation.surface: A crime writer's book belonged to a personified Time.
explanation.walkthrough: Josephine Tey's novel The Daughter of Time takes its title from the proverb 'Truth is the daughter of time'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tey's novel title makes truth the female child of time, so her book's subject belonged to Time.

clue.text: Loftier form of Benson work

indicators.note: form here means a new shape for the letters, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A grander version of a writer's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' signals an anagram of LOFTIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Trefoil is a book by Benson, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Goddess in heathen attachment

indicators.note: in shows the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A deity revered with pagan devotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to letters running across 'heathen attachment'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pallas was the Greek goddess of wisdom, patron of Athens.

clue.text: No, I'm not Byron (—)

parts.note: names the title of an 1832 poem by a Russian Romantic poet; the gap asks for its author

explanation.surface: Someone denies being the English Romantic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Mikhail Lermontov's poem 'No, I'm not Byron' sets him apart from the poet he was often compared with.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian poet Mikhail Lermontov wrote the 1832 lyric beginning 'No, I'm not Byron, I am another'.

clue.text: Writer on love is frank

indicators.note: on means the writer piece is placed after the love piece in the across entry

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: An author writing about romance is candid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts PEN after O.
explanation.definitionFit: Being open is being candid and honest, without concealment.

clue.text: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)

definitions.text: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)

parts.words: "When the past has latched its postern behind my tremulous —" (Thomas Hardy)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap; the missing word means a time of remaining or sojourn

explanation.surface: Hardy reflects on a life closing behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: The line opens Hardy's poem Afterwards, which pictures his death.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a word for a period of remaining somewhere, here Hardy's time on earth.

clue.text: Historic inspiration with cooking oil at start of century

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the following word
cooking means the letters are being worked into a new mix

explanation.surface: A recipe with oil at the dawn of a new century inspires historians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' rearranges the oil; 'at start of century' sets the first letter of 'century' before it. Clio is the Muse of history.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muse of history in Greek myth inspires historians, so she is the inspiration of history.

clue.text: Underworld second sight not inaccurately recalling old straits

parts.note: hell is the underworld
ESP, extrasensory perception, is second sight

indicators.note: inaccurately means the word is not set out correctly, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A vision of the underworld half-remembers an ancient sea passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inaccurately' turns NOT into ONT. The Dardanelles were called this in antiquity.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dardanelles were known by this name in antiquity, the narrow sea channel Leander swam.

clue.text: Direction taken by Rugby

parts.note: seems to be a compass bearing, but names Tom Brown's friend at Rugby School in Tom Brown's Schooldays

explanation.surface: Which way a school or town heads.
explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Hughes's Tom Brown's Schooldays, Harry East befriends Tom at Rugby School; he is also a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass point, and the surname of Harry, Tom Brown's companion at Rugby School.

clue.text: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson

definitions.text: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson

parts.words: Way of viewing subjects of Gorky, Phillpotts, Buck and Benson
parts.note: each writer produced a book titled after a parent of the female kind, so the answer is the adverb for viewing in that manner

explanation.surface: A survey of how four writers saw their subjects.
explanation.walkthrough: Gorky, Pearl Buck and others each wrote a novel called Mother; regarding things as such a person would is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Each writer has a novel called Mother, so to view those subjects is to look in a motherly way.
